tier_justification: Elementary predicate-logic facts, stated for satisfaction of sentences; they do not use the structure of formulas.
plain_claim: Let KM be a class of models, KS a class of systems and φ a sentence, with no map between model and system assumed. The statement 'for every model T in KM and every system R in KS, if φ holds in T then φ holds in R' is true exactly when φ is unsatisfiable in KM or valid in KS (`unrelated_truth_transfer_iff`). The statement 'for every model T in KM and every system R in KS, if φ fails in T then φ fails in R' is true exactly when φ is valid in KM or unsatisfiable in KS (`unrelated_falsity_transfer_iff`). The statement 'for every model T in KM and every system R in KS, if φ holds in T then φ fails in R' (reading a model result as a refutation) is true exactly when φ is unsatisfiable in KM or unsatisfiable in KS (`unrelated_refutation_licensed_iff`); for KM = KS = K, the statement 'for every T and every R in K, if φ holds in T then φ fails in R' is true exactly when φ is unsatisfiable in K (`unrelated_refutation_licensed_iff_unsat_same_class`). In each statement both quantifiers range over the whole implication: it says that for each model T of KM in which the premise holds, the conclusion holds in every system of KS. If φ holds in some model of KM and KS contains both a system satisfying φ and one falsifying it, then there is a model T of KM satisfying φ such that KS contains a system satisfying φ and a system falsifying φ, so this model result is consistent with both system outcomes (`unrelated_model_result_consistent_with_both`).

nonvacuity_witness: Over all structures (KM = KS), ∃x, P x is neither valid nor unsatisfiable and none of the three transfers is licensed (`unrelated_nonvacuous`); with KM = all structures and KS = the structures with non-empty carrier, for every model T of KM and every system R of KS, truth of ∃x, x = x in T implies its truth in R, because the system class decides it, although ∃x, x = x is neither valid nor unsatisfiable over all structures (`unrelated_two_class_example`).
non_claims: The characterizations depend on KM, KS and φ, not on a particular model or system. When the system class decides φ (ValidIn KS φ or UnsatIn KS φ), the system claim holds or fails for every system of KS regardless of the model.

The characterizations are about statements that quantify over every model of KM and every system of KS at once. They are not about the narrow-scope statement 'if φ holds in every model of KM then φ holds in every system of KS' (ValidIn KM φ → ValidIn KS φ), nor its falsity and refutation analogues, which are different statements: for KM = KS = all structures and φ = ∃x, P x each narrow-scope implication holds while the right-hand side of the corresponding characterization fails (`narrow_scope_readings_differ_from_unrelated_transfer`).

The same-class form allows the model and the system to be the same structure (T = R). If models and systems are known to come from different classes, use the two-class statements: then a refutation is licensed whenever φ is unsatisfiable in the system class, even if φ is satisfiable in the model class.
Says nothing about structures related by a map; for those, see the transfer matrix and `licences_exact`.

Structures may have empty carriers (`emptyStr`), unlike the classical convention of non-empty domains (Rossman 2008, §2.1.1). The statement quantifies over all structures, empty or not, so it also holds when structures are restricted to non-empty ones. Facts about validity do depend on the convention: `∃x, x = x` is not valid over all structures but is valid over the non-empty ones (`exSelfEq_valid_iff_nonempty_carriers`).

For a model class KM and a system class KS, a transfer statement over every model of KM and every system of KS holds exactly when the model class or the system class settles φ in the way given by the three characterizations.

Reasoning: reading a model result as a refutation of the system claim is the refutation statement of this card, and `unrelated_refutation_licensed_iff` shows that it holds exactly when φ is unsatisfiable in KM or unsatisfiable in KS; for a sentence that is satisfiable in KM and satisfiable in KS it does not hold, so such a reading is unlicensed. plain_claim: For every class c, map kind k and direction d, the cell (c, k, d) is unlicensed in the transfer table exactly when it admits both outcomes along non-isomorphisms (`bothOutcomesNonIso_iff_unlicensed`): there is a formula φ of class c (with parameters), a structure at the known end with an environment at which φ holds, and two k-maps, neither an isomorphism, such that φ holds at the other end of one and fails at the other end of the other. For a forward cell the known end is the source A with environment e, and φ is evaluated in each target at h ∘ e. For a backward cell the known end is the target B with environment b; each of the two maps h comes with a source environment e that it sends to b pointwise (h (e i) = b i for every i), and φ is evaluated in the source at that e. The two maps need not be distinct: in `both_eq` both outcomes use the map `collapse`, with two different source environments. Unlicensed does not mean that nothing transfers: model-side falsity is licensed while model-side truth is not for exactly seven (kind, orientation, class) triples (`falsity_licensed_where_truth_unlicensed_iff`), and some unlicensed cells contain proper subclasses that transfer (`unlicensed_cells_contain_transferring_subclasses`).

Strong homomorphisms license the same cells as homomorphisms because the signature includes equality: a non-injective strong homomorphism does not preserve `¬ x = y` (`neq_not_preserved_by_strongHom`) and does not reflect `x = y` (`eq_not_reflected_by_strongHom`). On equality-free quantifier-free formulas, strong homomorphisms do preserve and reflect satisfaction (`qf_sat_iff_of_strongHom_of_eqFree`). An equality-free version of the whole table is not formalized. 'Strong homomorphism' means `IsStrongHom` (preserves and reflects R and P); usage of the term varies in the literature.

The universal, existential, ∀∃ and ∃∀ classes are prenex, while the positive and positive existential classes allow quantifiers under ∧ and ∨. So a positive existential formula need not be existential in the prenex sense: `posExist_not_subset_exist` exhibits `(∃x, P x) ∧ (∃y, P y)`. Hodges (1993, §2.4) and Rossman (2008, Remark 2.1) use non-prenex classes. Classes are syntactic: a formula that is merely logically equivalent to a class member is not covered.

Structures may have empty carriers (`emptyStr`), unlike the classical convention of non-empty domains (Rossman 2008, §2.1.1). Every refuting instance in the table uses structures with one or two elements, and the licensed cells hold for all structures, so the table is unchanged if structures are restricted to non-empty ones (derived from the definitions of the countermodel structures; not stated as a separate theorem).
`.posExist` is listed separately from `.exist` because the positive existential class is not contained in the prenex existential class (`posExist_not_subset_exist`).
